claim: Titer needed for cost-efficient food protein by precision fermentation
value: above 50
notes: Nielsen MB, Meyer AS, Arnau J. Annu Rev Food Sci Technol 15:173-187 (online 2023, issue 2024). Wording: 'cost-efficiency requirements involve production titers above 50 g/L'. Assertion, not derived from a published TEA in the abstract. Prior lead 'Nielsen et al. 2023' is essentially correct (online-first 2023).

claim: Same authors repeat: 'Protein titers well above 50 g/L are needed'
value: well above 50
notes: Nielsen MB, Meyer AS, Hansen K. Industrial Biotechnology 22(2):131-140. Cites SCI-01 as source. Also states cost target USD 10/kg by 2025 and USD 1/kg by 2035 ('envisaged'). Absolute titer not disclosed (feed data confidential; titer confidentiality only implied); reports protein production raised by almost 80% and a carbon yield above 70% vs centre point at pH 6.9, 36 C.

claim: Secreted leghemoglobin titer in Pichia pastoris
fulltext_read: N (closed; value via citing paper SCI-04)
notes: Shao Y et al. Bioresource Technology 363:127884. Value confirmed as cited by Tian et al. 2024 ('secretory expression ... titer of 3.5 g/L').

claim: Intracellular leghemoglobin titer in Kluyveromyces marxianus
notes: Tian T et al. Front Bioeng Biotechnol 11:1329016 (published 2024). 80% above parent strain (4.04 g/L). Authors call it the highest intracellular LBA titer reported to that date. Intracellular, so needs cell disruption.

claim: Leghemoglobin titer after process optimisation in K. marxianus
notes: Chen H et al. Biotechnology Journal 21(5). Up from 6.13 g/L at initial conditions (+64.7%). Current best published LBA titer found in this review. Still about 5x below the 50 g/L bulk-protein benchmark (our calculation), but heme proteins are used at low inclusion in a product so the benchmark is less binding.

claim: T. reesei food-protein host: reported titers
value: 1 (beta-lactoglobulin); 2 (ovalbumin)
notes: Aro N et al. Food Research International 163:112131 (2023 issue; online November 2022). Abstract reports 1 g/L beta-lactoglobulin and 2 g/L ovalbumin; full text not read.

claim: T. reesei single heterologous protein yield (VTT, unpublished)
value: above 80
notes: Mojzita D, Aro N et al. Front Bioeng Biotechnol 13:1688495. Claim is 'VTT, unpublished data'. Same paper: brazzein 1.3 g/L in 250 mL bioreactor; cost estimate EUR 57-80/kg brazzein at 1.3 g/L.

claim: OPENPichia chassis licence terms
value: royalty-free commercial manufacture; liberal end-user distribution licences; toolkit free of third-party MTAs
retraction_check: none found (1 contrasting citation, not a notice)
notes: Claes K et al. Nature Microbiology 9(3):864-876. Distributed by VIB (OPENPichia.com) with NCYC. Not literally 'licence-free': users accept a liberal licence. Strain is near-identical to NRRL Y-11430; no strain consistently better; HOC1 truncation restores transformability.

claim: EFSA opinion: soy leghemoglobin from GM K. phaffii as a food additive (colour in meat analogues)
value: opinion issued
notes: EFSA FAF Panel, EFSA Journal 22(6):e8822. Safety of GM aspect assessed separately by GMO Panel (EFSA-GMO-NL-2019-162). Check final conclusion before quoting.

claim: ICAR-NBFGR striped catfish thymus continuous cell line 'PHT' exists
value: PHT, NRFC-078; 52 passages; L-15 + 20% FBS; 28 C; 2n=60; epithelial
notes: Soni P, Pradhan PK, Sood N et al. Indian J Anim Sci 93(2). Deposited at National Repository of Fish Cell Lines, ICAR-NBFGR Lucknow. Purpose: virology, toxicology, transgenics. Not a food cell line: serum-dependent (20% FBS), adherent, epithelial, not myogenic or adipogenic. Transfer to VN: same species as VN tra catfish.

claim: Striped catfish gill cell line exists (lead called it 'PHG')
value: gill line published; name 'PHG' not confirmed in record read
notes: Sathiyanarayanan A, Goswami M, Nagpure NS et al. Fish Physiol Biochem 48(2):367-380 (ICAR authors). Also a caudal fin line: Soni P et al. 2018 Acta Tropica 182:215-222 (10.1016/j.actatropica.2018.03.015), and a skin epithelial line from Taiwan (Wu & Wang 2025/2026, 10.1016/j.fsi.2025.110836). All disease-research lines.

claim: Shrimp-insect hybrid cell line 'PmLyO-Sf9' exists
value: PmLyO-Sf9: P. monodon lymphoid cells fused with insect Sf9 line
organism_or_product: Penaeus monodon x Spodoptera frugiperda Sf9 hybrid
notes: Anoop BS, Puthumana J et al. Fish Shellfish Immunol 113:196-207. From Cochin University of Science and Technology group (I.S. Bright Singh), NOT ICAR-NBFGR (prior lead implied NBFGR). Contains insect genome: not a shrimp food cell line. Used for WSSV and IHHNV virology (SCI-13). Black tiger shrimp, not whiteleg shrimp. No true continuous shrimp cell line exists in the literature found.

claim: Humbird: practical max cell density in suspension
value: 258 (absolute max); 110 fed-batch; 140 single ATF perfusion; 195 O2-limited perfusion
notes: Humbird D. Biotechnol Bioeng 118(8):3239-3250. With inefficient metabolism ammonia inhibition caps density at 7-20 g/L. Conclusion: economics 'would likely preclude the affordability' of cultured meat as food.

claim: Humbird: growth factor cost contribution at 100 kt/yr scale
notes: Assumes large-scale recombinant production prices. Contrast with current-price estimates that growth factors are up to 95% of serum-free medium cost (SCI-15). Both are true under different price assumptions; do not average.

claim: Share of serum-free medium cost from growth factors at current prices
value: up to 95
notes: Dolgin J et al. 2026 preprint (openRxiv), citing Stout et al. and Negulescu et al. 2023 (10.1002/bit.28324: media ~98% of raw material cost at scale). Preprint; secondary statement.

claim: Achieved density in animal-free medium (chicken cells, continuous culture)
notes: Pasitka L et al. Nature Food 2024. Up to 130 million cells/mL (reported as a 43% w/v yield) with repeated harvests over 20 days, in animal-component-free medium costing USD 0.63/L; the same paper models USD 6.2/lb (about USD 13.67/kg) for a 50,000 L perfusion facility. A 2025 review (SCI-17) gives 28 million cells/mL and a 38% cut in medium cost. The 43% w/v yield is above Humbird's 140-195 g/L; bases may differ, not reconciled. No comparable data for fish or shrimp cells.

claim: Karimi 2019: A. oryzae 'biomass yield' on 5% vinasse
value: 118.5 (reported); broth-basis value implied by COD mass balance about 5.9
organism_or_product: A. oryzae CBS 819.72 on molasses vinasse
scale: 250 mL shake flask, 100 mL, 72 h, 35 C
notes: Karimi S et al. Fermentation 5(4):99. Methods: 100 mL of 5% (v/v) vinasse, biomass sieved (1 mm2), washed, oven-dried at 70 C. Medium COD stated as about 21 g/L. 11.85 g dry biomass from 100 mL holding about 2.1 g COD is impossible, so 118.5 cannot be a broth concentration. The paper reports COD on an as-received vinasse basis (835 g/L) and cites a related study in 'g per litre of vinasse'. Most plausible reading: per litre of undiluted vinasse, i.e. about 5.9 g/L in the flask (118.5 x 0.05; my arithmetic). Paper does not state the basis explicitly and is internally inconsistent (835 x 5% = 42, not 21 g/L COD). Do NOT use 118.5 g/L as a titer or productivity input. Protein (N x 6.25): A. oryzae 44.7%, N. intermedia 57.6%, R. oryzae 50.9%.

claim: A. oryzae mycotoxin potential
value: cannot make aflatoxin (disabling mutations in cluster); CAN make cyclopiazonic acid (CPA) and 3-nitropropionic acid; kojic acid is not classed as a mycotoxin
notes: Frisvad JC et al. Appl Microbiol Biotechnol 102:9481-9515. Modern industrial strains carry a large deletion removing the aflatoxin cluster and CPA genes; CPA cluster can be deleted (Kato 2011). Reports of aflatoxigenic 'A. oryzae' are misidentified A. flavus. Implication: a koji/biomass play must use a characterised strain with CPA/3-NPA testing; wild tuong starter cultures are not automatically safe.

claim: Mycoprotein RNA content before and after heat treatment
value: about 10 -> about 2
notes: Coelho MOC et al. Nutrients 12(4):1115. Heat treatment 68 C for 20 min lets endogenous enzymes degrade RNA; described as 'industrially expensive'. Meets FAO/WHO/UNICEF PAG guidance. Protein of F. venenatum mycoprotein is 30-45% DW in a 2025 review (SCI-21, secondary).

claim: Protein content range of SCP by organism group
value: bacteria up to 65; F. venenatum 30-45
notes: D'Almeida AP, de Albuquerque TL. Fermentation 11(1):24. Also: thermal RNA reduction to <1% 'to be considered safe' (wording varies between sources; SCI-20 says ~2%).

claim: Candida utilis crude protein on cassava peel hydrolysate
value: 47.5 (glucose); 49.1 (acid hydrolysate); 56.7 (enzymatic hydrolysate)
notes: Ezekiel OO, Aworh OC, du Preez JC. J Food Sci Eng 2(8). Prior claim '49-57%' is correct. Yield 0.44-0.52 g/g sugar. Cardinal temperatures 14/33/41 C (max 41 C). N x 6.25 includes nucleic-acid N (yeast RNA 6-12%), so true protein is lower. Publisher (David Publishing) is low-tier; treat as indicative. Nigerian cassava peel, transferable to VN cassava residues with caution.

claim: CAP (Clostridium autoethanogenum protein) at 30% of a whiteleg shrimp test diet: growth not different from control and higher protein digestibility (a digestibility trial, not a fishmeal replacement test)
organism_or_product: CAP (steel-mill CO gas fermentation), L. vannamei
notes: Li X et al. Aquaculture Nutrition 2022:8225273 (SCI-23), apparent digestibility of six novel proteins in L. vannamei. The earlier cited doi:10.1016/j.aqrep.2021.100938 is a largemouth bass study, not shrimp. CAP lysine-rich.

claim: Halving fishmeal (25% -> 12.5% of diet) with CAP reduced shrimp growth unless a bile acid (CDCA 0.06%) was added
value: growth reduced at 50% FM replacement without CDCA
notes: Shi M et al. Animals 13(13):2109. Shows a ceiling near 30-50% FM replacement for CAP in shrimp without additives.

claim: Digestibility/growth screen at 30% test-ingredient inclusion in shrimp: methanotroph bacterial meal (BPM) and BSF/mealworm reduced growth; CAP and Chlorella did not
value: BPM protein ADC lower than control; CAP protein ADC higher than control
organism_or_product: Methylococcus capsulatus Bath meal (71% CP), CAP, BSF larvae meal, Chlorella, L. vannamei
notes: Li X et al. Aquaculture Nutrition 2022:8225273. Note 30% of whole diet is a high inclusion, not a fishmeal-replacement trial. Also reports prior findings: BSF can replace 20% FM without harm; Chlorella 75% FM (secondary).

claim: Microbial community SCP from soybean-processing wastewater replaced fishmeal in whiteleg shrimp
value: up to 90 (growth maintained); survival high to 100
unit: % of fishmeal replaced (up to 220 g SCP/kg feed)
scale: 4 trials, 42-84 days, lab and pilot SCP
notes: Santillan E et al. 2025 preprint (openRxiv), Singapore-based authors. Directly relevant to VN tofu/soy-milk wastewater. Not yet peer reviewed.

claim: Brewer's yeast replaced fishmeal in hybrid 'Thai Panga' catfish with improved growth and immunity
organism_or_product: brewer's yeast, Pangasianodon hypophthalmus x Pangasius bocourti
notes: Sultana S et al. Animals 14(19):2851 review, citing primary study. Pangasius diets use little fishmeal (prior lead 2-5%), so in pangasius SCP competes mainly with soybean meal, not fishmeal. S. cerevisiae reported without detriment in Nile tilapia.

claim: Black soldier fly larvae meal replacing fishmeal in whiteleg shrimp
value: 20% FM replacement no growth loss; 30% FM replacement reduced growth
unit: % of fishmeal protein replaced (control diet 25% FM)
notes: Chen Y et al. Br J Nutr 128(9):1674-1688. BSF at 9.5% of the diet replaced 20% of fishmeal protein, about 5% of the diet as fishmeal (control diet 25% FM). Benchmark: BSF displaces little fishmeal in shrimp; SCI-23 also found reduced growth and lower protein digestibility for BSF meal.

claim: EFSA opinion on Wolffia globosa powder (Mankai-type NF): safety could not be established
value: safety cannot be established (manganese intake concern); NOAEL 6.5 g/kg bw/day; possible allergenicity
organism_or_product: Wolffia globosa powder, controlled cultivation, hot-water washed, dried
notes: EFSA NDA Panel, EFSA Journal 19(12):6938. Trace elements and contaminants depend strongly on cultivation water and fertiliser. A 2026 review (SCI-31) states the NF was later authorised by Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2223; NOT verified (EUR-Lex fetch blocked). Treat EU authorisation status as open.

claim: EFSA opinion on water lentil powder (Lemna 70-100%, Wolffia 0-30%)
value: safety cannot be established (manganese)
notes: EFSA NDA Panel, EFSA Journal 19(11):6845. Same Mn issue.

claim: EFSA opinion on water lentil protein CONCENTRATE (L. gibba + L. minor)
value: safe under proposed uses; low allergy risk
organism_or_product: Lemna protein concentrate (fibre removed, pasteurised, spray-dried)
notes: EFSA NDA Panel, EFSA Journal 21(4):7903. Lesson: extracting protein removes the Mn problem that blocked whole-plant powders.

claim: Fresh Wolffia plants deemed 'not novel' in the EU
value: NOT VERIFIED
notes: EC 'consultation process on novel food status' page fetched; no Wolffia entry seen in the (possibly truncated) listing. Mes et al. 2022 (SCI-33) state 'all genera of duckweed are classified as Novel Food' by EFSA. Position: do not claim fresh Wolffia is non-novel in the EU until the EC catalogue entry is read.

claim: Wolffia protein content (11 species, axenic lab culture)
notes: Appenroth KJ et al. Front Chem 6:483. Fibre ~25%, starch 10-20%, fat 1-5%. EAA ratios vs WHO preschool pattern at or above ~1 (amino acid score, NOT digestibility-corrected). Mn 78-431 mg/kg FDW in 16 samples.

claim: Crude protein and in vitro digestibility of Thai duckweeds
value: Wolffia 44.3; Lemna 22.2; Spirodela 18.0 (% DM CP); in vitro SIDCP Lemna 72%, Wolffia 69%, Spirodela 39%
notes: Thongthung H et al. Trends in Sciences 21(11):8324. Protein varies 2x with species and water nutrients; in vitro digestibility only.

claim: Duckweed productivity
value: about 30 (average, cited); 33 t DM/ha over 8 months in domestic wastewater; 'up to 100' t DM/ha/yr is an extrapolated upper bound
notes: Salian A et al. J Anim Sci Biotechnol 17 (2026) review; the same review prints '102.5 t/ha/d', an evident error, so treat its numbers with care. 'Up to 100 t DM/ha/yr' appears in Pagliuso et al. 2022 preprint citing Ziegler 2015. No VN field data. Use 10-30 t DM/ha/yr as a planning range pending VN trials (my judgement).

claim: 'PDCAAS 0.89' for duckweed/Wolffia
value: NOT FOUND in peer-reviewed literature searched
notes: No duckweed PDCAAS or DIAAS study found via Scite. Appenroth 2018 reports amino acid scores only. Human data: L. minor protein absorbed less than pea protein (Mes et al., cited in SCI-33). Drop the 0.89 figure unless a primary source is produced.

claim: Microalgae DIAAS data availability
value: no DIAAS for microalgal biomass available (as of 2021 review)
notes: Wang Y, Tibbetts SM, McGinn PJ. Foods 10(12):3002. Spirulina protein content and digestibility figures were not verified in this wave.

claim: DIAAS of protein ingredients (growing pigs; older child/adult pattern)
value: soy isolate 97; pea concentrate 70; brown rice concentrate 42 (0.5-3 y: soy 83; pea 60)
organism_or_product: soy protein isolate, pea protein concentrate, brown rice protein concentrate
notes: Bailey HM, Fanelli NS, Stein HH. J Sci Food Agric 103(14):7251-7259. Limiting AA: lysine (rice), sulfur AA (soy, pea). Rice and pea concentrates DIAAS <75.

claim: DIAAS of cooked mung bean (growing pigs)
value: 68 (0.5-3 y); 86 (older child/adult)
notes: Han F, Moughan PJ et al. Nutrients 12(12):3831. Peas 57/68. Lysine limiting for young child pattern; leucine for older.

claim: True ileal IAA digestibility measured in children (dual isotope)
value: mung bean 65.2%; rice 78.5%; egg 87.4%
notes: Shivakumar N et al. Am J Clin Nutr 109(5):1319-1327. Mung bean digestibility in children about 20% lower than pig values. Typical cereal-legume complementary diets DIAAS about 80; adding egg or milk raised it to 100 (calculated).

claim: Measured rice+legume blend DIAAS >= 100
value: NONE FOUND
notes: Only CALCULATED values found: pea+rice blends with 40-90% pea can reach PDCAAS 1.00 on the adult pattern (Hertzler 2020, cited in Nichele et al. 2022); potato+fava+corn and pea+wheat meals reach DIAAS 100 (Herreman 2020, calculated). No measured (in vivo) rice+legume blend DIAAS >= 100 was found.

claim: Thermotolerant K. marxianus grows at 35-45 C; high-density biomass on raw cassava starch
value: 39.3 g/L (3.28 g/L/h) single batch; 36-46 g/L repeated batch
organism_or_product: K. marxianus SS106 (isolated from Thai cassava pulp and starch-factory soil)
notes: Malairuang K et al. Processes 8(8):898. Chose 40 C over 42 C for energy saving. Directly transferable to VN cassava starch factories.

claim: Cooling-cost saving from high-temperature fermentation
value: qualitative only ('expected to reduce cooling cost'); no quantified tropical cooling-cost analysis found
notes: Lertwattanasakul N et al. Biotechnol Biofuels 8:47. Wave 1 cost agent estimated USD 70-180/t biomass for chilled water in southern VN (own estimate, not peer reviewed). K. marxianus is also a precision-fermentation host (SCI-04, SCI-05: leghemoglobin 7-10 g/L) and C. utilis tolerates up to 41 C (SCI-22).

claim: Drum-dried Wolffia globosa protein and in vitro digestibility
value: protein 32-34% DW; IVPD 81% fresh -> 85% dried
notes: Pattarayingsakul W et al. J Sci Food Agric 106(4):2242-2250. In vitro only. Review statement in the same paper: Wolffia 20-45% protein DW.
